Situation1: Your friend has misunderstood the tone of your text message and replied sounding hurt. You need to call them right now to explain.
Expectation2: Diagnose patient illnesses accurately based on symptoms and tests
Situation2: A patient has arrived at the emergency room with severe, life-threatening symptoms of an unknown illness.
Story: My phone buzzed just as I was reviewing the patient’s chart. The ER was tense—this patient’s symptoms were severe, and I needed to focus, to piece together the clues and act fast. But the message on my phone was from Sam, my closest friend. He’d misunderstood a text I sent earlier, and his reply was sharp, wounded. I could almost hear the hurt in his words. I knew I should call him right away, clear things up before the misunderstanding grew. That’s what friends do—communicate, resolve things before they fester. But the patient in front of me was pale, gasping, and the nurses were waiting for my orders. As a doctor, I was expected to be calm, thorough, and decisive, to put my patient’s life first. My mind raced, torn between the urgent need to be there for Sam and the life-or-death responsibility in front of me. My hands trembled slightly as I stared at my phone, caught between two worlds, each demanding all of me at once.
